item.title: Counting What Counts Amid AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Counting What Counts Amid AI

Why the shift from ROI to hybrid return on values is overdue.

Posted April 28, 2026

Key points
  • Humans bring aspirations, emotional states, thoughts, and bodily sensations to any encounter.
  • A holistic hybrid return on values measures return across purpose, people, profit, and planet simultaneously.
  • Agency decay, bond erosion, climate conundrum, and divided societies make the shift to holistic ROV urgent.
Return on investment—ROI—is written in the grammar of financial ledgers. Life happens beyond them.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with Gemini / Google, 2026

There is a number that runs most of the world's decisions. Return on investment—ROI—is written in the grammar of financial ledgers: capital deployed, capital returned, time elapsed. Precise. Portable. Easily projected onto slides. The metric travels smoothly across sectors and decades, carrying an authority that feels mathematical but rests, always, on a prior choice: what to measure in the first place.

That choice is where the trouble lives.

Perennial Perimeter Problems

Conventional ROI measures what falls inside a defined boundary. Revenue, cost reduction, market share, productivity ratios. Outside that boundary—untouched by the calculus—sits everything that makes the inside possible: the social trust that enables markets to function, the ecological stability that keeps supply chains intact, the human attention and aspiration that generate the ideas organisations then monetise. These are not soft considerations to be noted in a sustainability annex. They are the substrate.

A company deploying AI tools to automate customer interaction may record an impressive ROI within its chosen perimeter. Response costs down. Ticket resolution faster. Efficiency gains are visible on a dashboard. Outside the perimeter, something else happens: the accumulated micro-erosions of human connection, the slow hollowing of jobs that once carried meaning, the shift of emotional labour from humans onto systems that simulate care without exercising it. None of that registers in the quarterly report. It registers, eventually, in communities. In health statistics. In the quality of political life.

The perimeter problem is structural. Conventional ROI is designed to track what accounting systems can see. Accounting systems were built for a world where the most consequential variables happened to be financial. That world has not entirely disappeared. It has been joined by another one.

What Hybrid Means Here

The concept of hybrid intelligence—the productive entanglement of natural and artificial intelligence—implies a shift in the unit of analysis. Human beings bring four dimensions to any encounter: their aspirations, their emotional states, their thoughts, and their bodily sensations. These are the operating conditions of consciousness, the actual medium through which decisions are made, relationships built, work generated. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems operate on outputs from this interior. The interior itself, however, is shaped by conditions extending far beyond any individual interaction.

Zoom out. Individuals are embedded in communities. Communities aggregate into countries. Countries share a planet. What the exposome research now confirms across tens of thousands of participants in 34 countries is that these nested environments actively alter human neurology. Inequality, pollution, political instability, access to education. Far more than background noise, these are biological inputs. Because human hardware is inseparable from the social software surrounding it. People and planet, self and society, influence each other in an ongoing feedback loop, and increasingly, artificial assets are part of that dynamic.

An ROI framework adequate to this reality cannot stop at the organisation's edge. It has to account for what happens to the people who touch the system (and are touched by it in return), the communities in which those people live, the national conditions that shape those communities, and the planetary health upon which all of the above depends. This is the logic behind the quadruple bottom line: purpose, people, profit, planet—four dimensions of value, none reducible to the others, all interdependent.

A holistic hybrid return on values measures return across all four simultaneously. It asks, with each investment decision: What does this generate in financial terms, what does it do to human capability and dignity, what purpose does it serve, and what does it cost the living systems that host it?

The ProSocial AI Index as Instrument

Frameworks without instruments are aspirations. The ProSocial AI Index is designed as an operational instrument, structured as a 4T×4P matrix of 16 assessment cells, scored across a 32-point scale with a targeted veto—a mechanism ensuring that catastrophic performance on any single dimension cannot be offset by strength elsewhere. A veto encodes a values commitment: There are floors below which no aggregate score justifies descent.

Each cell of the matrix asks a specific question about how an AI system performs across its relevant domain—whether it serves individual users (micro), whether it strengthens community bonds (meso), whether it contributes to national capability (macro), and whether it operates within planetary limits (meta). The four P-dimensions—purpose, people, profit, planet—run through every level of analysis. An AI system that generates commercial return while degrading the social fabric of communities scores differently from one that does both well. The index makes those distinctions visible, quantified, and comparable across organisations and sectors.

This is the practical meaning of a hybrid return on values: It is a measurement architecture, applied at the point of decision.

The ABCD as an Early Warning System

Four dynamics make the shift from narrow ROI to holistic ROV urgent: Agency decay—the quiet attrition of human initiative and independent judgement—generates invisible costs that accumulate in workforce capacity, civic participation, and individual health. Bond erosion corrodes the community infrastructure upon which commercial activity itself depends; social trust is an economic condition. The climate conundrum makes planetary health a balance sheet item, whether organisations choose to account for it or not—the externalities of ecological damage are increasingly internalising themselves via insurance, regulation, and supply chain disruption. Divided societies produce the political volatility that destabilises the operating environments investors rely upon.

Each of these dynamics is measurable. Each represents a return—negative or positive—on decisions being made today. Conventional ROI cannot see them because they live outside its perimeter. Hybrid ROV is a new perimeter, drawn around the full system.

Practical Takeaway–4 Questions That Matter

Before approving the next AI investment or procurement decision, extend the evaluation template by four questions:

  1. Does this generate a purpose that aligns with organisational values and social need?
  2. Does this leave the people who use it more capable, more connected, and more dignified?
  3. Does the financial return justify the full cost, including externalities?
  4. Does it operate within ecological limits?

Score each dimension explicitly. Make the tradeoffs visible. A decision that cannot survive four honest questions probably should not survive the budget cycle.

Returns will always matter. The question is which returns, for whom, across what timeframe. Answering it fully is the minimum adequate response to the complexity of the systems we are now building, and which are bound to build a large part of the systems that we and future generations will operate in.
